text: Lesson 5 established that every relationship between two CIs is a real row on cmdb_rel_ci, directional and typed. The Dependency View is the platform's visual way of looking at those rows for one specific CI — open it from a CI record, and it lays out that CI's upstream and downstream relationships as a graph.

It's worth being precise about what the Dependency View actually is. It isn't a separate data source, and it doesn't calculate anything new — it's a graphical read of exactly the same relationship data you'd see by querying cmdb_rel_ci directly. If the underlying relationships are missing or wrong, the Dependency View will faithfully show that same missing or wrong picture.

Everything in Lesson 5 — creating a relationship record by hand, picking the right type — is manual relationship documentation, the same basic mechanism this path's Platform Fundamentals course taught with reference fields and related lists, just applied at CMDB scale. It's simple to set up, but the real cost is ongoing upkeep: every time something changes, a human has to remember to update the records.

Service Mapping is a real, separately available capability, similar in spirit to how Performance Analytics and IntegrationHub are also add-ons layered on top of the base platform. Instead of a person documenting that an application runs on a server, Service Mapping discovers the relationship automatically by tracing real network traffic and process-level connections between components of a business service.

Pointed at a business service, Service Mapping can trace outward from a known entry point, like a load balancer, through the real application and database tiers underneath it, discovering CIs and relationships nobody had to type in by hand. It's more powerful, but it's a bigger investment — credentials, configuration, and typically its own license.

Neither approach is simply better. Manual documentation is cheap but decays as an environment grows; Service Mapping stays current but costs more to run. Most mature instances use both. Next: using this relationship graph for real impact analysis — what actually breaks when one CI goes down.
